<explanation>
Based on our analysis of both the file tree and README, Dagu is a compact, single-binary workflow engine that supports declarative workflow definitions (using YAML) and provides a real-time web UI for monitoring execution. The project combines a robust backend written in Go with a modern React-based frontend interface—all packaged to run locally without external dependencies. Here’s how to draft an accurate and detailed system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   - Backend Engine: Represent the core “engine” (the binary started from cmd/main.go) which includes several subcomponents:
     • Workflow Parser & Executor: The modules under internal/digraph and internal/config that read DAG YAML files, build dependency graphs, and manage execution flows.
     • Task Executors: Components in internal/digraph/executor (for Docker, SSH, HTTP, jq, mail, etc.) that provide different execution mechanisms.
     • Scheduler: The scheduling logic (see internal/scheduler and scheduler jobs) that determines when tasks should run based on cron schedules.
     • Persistence & Logging: File-based storage components (internal/persistence/jsondb, internal/persistence/local, internal/logger) managing state, logs, and output.
     • Agent & Command Interface: Modules for handling CLI commands (cmd and internal/cmd) and interactions with the agent (internal/agent) that monitors workflow state.
   - Web UI: The frontend served from the “ui” directory, built with TypeScript/React. It handles rendering of workflows, live updates of logs/status (using routes defined in internal/frontend/server and assets under ui/src).
   - API Layer: The REST API (generated in internal/frontend/gen/restapi) provides endpoints that the UI consumes to show real-time status, logs, and configuration details.
   - Supporting Tools & Configuration: Tools such as the Dockerfile, docker-compose.yaml, and various configuration files support deployment and containerization, while docs and examples help users understand the system.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   - The Web UI communicates with the backend’s API endpoints to fetch real-time DAG statuses, execution logs, and to submit new workflow requests.
   - When a user initiates a DAG via the UI or CLI, the engine reads the YAML configuration, builds the DAG (using components in internal/digraph), and triggers the appropriate executors.
   - The Scheduler component periodically checks for scheduled workflows and triggers execution.
   - Outputs from one step are passed into subsequent tasks via a well-defined “data passing” mechanism (note the use of output variables).
   - Notification and logging components (mailer, logger) record execution details and may interact externally (e.g., sending email notifications or HTTP requests).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   - Monolithic Single Binary: Despite having distinct logical modules, everything is compiled into one executable without an external dependency, contributing to a “local-first” design.
   - Declarative Configuration: The system is built around YAML-defined workflows, making the execution flow clear and maintainable.
   - Modular Design: Though in one binary, the code is well separated into packages (scheduler, executor, persistence, logger), each responsible for a specific function.
   - Client-Server Separation: Even in a local deployment, the separation between the API backend and React-based UI is clear. Use distinct colors/shapes to demarcate backend modules versus frontend/client components.

4. Include Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   - Backend is implemented in Go. Note the use of Go’s package structure (cmd, internal packages) and tools like Goreleaser for builds.
   - The UI is built with React (TypeScript/TSX files) and bundled with Webpack.
   - Configuration parsers and workflow engines (YAML processing, JSON databases) are integral parts of how workflows are executed.
   - Tools such as Docker and docker-compose are also featured for containerized deployment.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   - As this is a full-stack orchestration engine with a single binary deployment, clearly distinguish between the frontend (Web UI) and the backend (which includes execution, scheduling, and persistence).
   - Emphasize the DAG processing pipeline: show how a YAML workflow is ingested, parsed into a directed acyclic graph, scheduled, and executed through various executors.
   - Highlight communication flows between components: illustrate the API calls from the UI to backend endpoints, the data flow from scheduler to executor, and real-time log streaming.
   - Make sure to annotate which parts are “local” (e.g., file-based persistence) and which might interface with external services (mail notifications, HTTP requests).

6. Instruct on Diagram Elements:
   - Use clear, descriptive labels for each component (e.g., “Workflow Parser & Executor”, “Task Scheduler”, “API Server”, “React Web UI”, “Persistence Module”).
   - Draw directional arrows to indicate data flow or control flow:
       • From “User/CLI” to “API Server” illustrating workflow submission.
       • From “API Server” to “Workflow Executor” showing task execution initiation.
       • Multi-directional arrows between “Scheduler” and “Executor” to show timing and dependency management.
       • Arrows indicating the channel of notifications (for instance, from the “Mailer” module to external systems).
   - Use distinct colors/shapes to differentiate backend components from frontend elements and external modules (for example, backend modules could be rectangles while the UI is in a rounded rectangle or a dashed boundary to denote its role as an interface).

7. Detail the Overall Diagram Layout:
   - At the top, place the User Interface (both CLI and Web UI) as the entry point.
   - Center the diagram with the core backend engine subdivided into clusters: Workflow Engine (including parser, DAG builder, and scheduler), Executor modules, Persistence, and Logging.
   - Alongside, depict the API layer that bridges the backend and the Web UI.
   - In a separate box (or attached note), include deployment / containerization details like Docker and configuration files if relevant.

By following these detailed guidelines, you—as the principal software engineer—can produce an accurate, comprehensive system design diagram that captures the architectural elements of Dagu. The resulting diagram will clearly represent the separation of concerns, data/control flow between components, and the modular structure of this compact workflow engine.
</explanation>
